title: About these options
docsLink: Read the detailed guide on the website
skipVerify: Enable when the backend uses HTTPS with a self-signed or expired certificate, such as the https port of a NAS or router admin page. The backend identity is no longer verified, so use it only for LAN backends.
targetHost: By default the domain the visitor used is passed to the backend unchanged. Enable when the backend only accepts its own address, e.g. it returns 400 / 403, redirects to the wrong address or reports a Host mismatch; usually needed when proxying to public services.
noKeepAlive: By default connections to the backend are reused to cut latency. Enable when the backend sometimes resets connections, requests hang, or it does not support keep-alive; every request then opens a new connection.
forwarded: Tells the backend the visitor's real IP and source port, the original scheme (http / https), the host and the access port (X-Real-IP, X-Real-Port, X-Forwarded-*). Enable it when the backend logs real IPs and ports or needs to know the outside is HTTPS to build correct links; recommended for most apps.
sendProxy: Prepends a PROXY protocol header to the connection to pass the real IP, for backends that do not read HTTP headers, such as another Gately, haproxy or nginx with proxy_protocol. Backends not configured to accept it fail outright, so leave it off if unsure. When on, every request opens a new connection and HTTP/2 to the backend is not used. If the backend is Gately, turn on accepting the PROXY protocol on its listener and add this host to its trusted PROXY sources.
sniFromHost: HTTPS backends only: sends the domain the visitor used during the handshake and verifies the certificate against it. Enable when the backend selects certificates or routes by domain on one port, such as frp vhost_https or an nginx hosting several HTTPS sites.
passAuthCookies: By default Gately removes its own sign-in cookies (single sign-on, site session, third-party sign-in) so sign-in credentials are not handed to the backend app. Enable when the backend is another Gately that handles authentication, for example a public Gately that only does WAF and access control in front of a LAN Gately that handles sign-in. Not available while this site has authentication enabled. Only use it when the backend is your own Gately: an ordinary app that receives these cookies could reuse the visitor's sign-in.
